name: Neoliberalism
summary: Neoliberalism holds that competitive markets, secure private property and a rule-of-law state limited by general rules are the best basis for freedom and prosperity. Its branches favour free trade, privatization, deregulation, sound money, broad-based low-rate taxes and a modest safety net in place of an extensive welfare state, and distrust central planning and concentrated political power. They differ on money, conscription, healthcare and unions.
scope: A family entry, answering only what independent branches share: the Austrian and Mont Pelerin strand (Hayek, The Road to Serfdom, the 1947 Statement of Aims, read through Miller's account of The Constitution of Liberty), the Chicago school (Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom), the Virginia public-choice school (Buchanan, through the Stanford Encyclopedia and Econlib, whose primary texts were not available to open) and the Washington Consensus (Williamson's 1990 statement of the reforms Washington institutions urged). Ordoliberalism, Thatcherism, authoritarian neoliberalism, classical liberalism and libertarianism have their own entries and are excluded, as is the pejorative catch-all use of the word. A position needs two branches that state it independently and none stating the opposite; Friedman- or Hayek-only positions are null.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The record is mixed: Hayek accepts compulsory health insurance and public assistance for the needy but opposes state medicine, while Friedman lists medical care programs among welfare measures he opposes.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The sources record no position shared by the school's branches on this question, and no stated principle settles it.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Statement of Aims ties freedom to the competitive market, Hayek's Road to Serfdom argues competition beats central direction, Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom makes the market the main means of cooperation, and Williamson reports the Washington view that private industry is run more efficiently than state firms.

public-ownership.rationale: Friedman lists publicly run toll roads, national parks and publicly operated annuity systems among activities liberal principles cannot justify, Williamson reports privatization as an article of faith in Washington, and the Statement of Aims ties freedom to private property and the competitive market.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Hayek treats progressive income tax as a major threat to freedom and Friedman finds no justification for graduation solely to redistribute, while Williamson reports a broad consensus for a broad tax base with moderate marginal rates.

unions-good.rationale: Hayek argues unions raise their members' wages by coercion at the cost of other workers and of the Rule of Law, and Friedman treats labour unions as a form of monopoly power to be met with antitrust action.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Statement of Aims names decline of belief in private property as a cause of the crisis, Hayek holds it essential against coercion but allows expropriation at fair market value for amenities, and Williamson notes general acceptance that property rights matter.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Friedman lists detailed industry regulation as unjustified and Williamson reports deregulation as the consensus goal, while Hayek accepts some regulation (building rules, natural monopolies) and so only mildly opposes.

missingStatements.text: Governments should eliminate subsidies to industry and agriculture.
missingStatements.rationale: Friedman lists farm price supports first among unjustified activities, Hayek calls farm subsidies compulsory transfers, and Williamson reports indiscriminate subsidies as prime candidates for elimination.

missingStatements.text: State-owned enterprises should be sold to private owners.
missingStatements.rationale: Williamson reports privatization as official US policy since 1985 and an article of faith in Washington, and Friedman lists publicly operated toll roads and annuity systems as unjustified.

missingStatements.text: Governments should avoid fixing prices and wages by decree.
missingStatements.rationale: Friedman says price controls would end free enterprise and Hayek opposes administrative direction of prices and wages; Williamson lists price controls among harmful regulations.

notes: Neoliberalism is audited here as a family, so only positions shared by independent branches are answered; most social and cultural statements are null. Splits recorded as 0: universal healthcare, conscription, compulsory union membership, abolishing central banks and inheritance tax. Buchanan is read only through the Stanford Encyclopedia and Econlib because his books were not openly available (the Liberty Fund and Nobel pages refused automated access and were not circumvented), so no answer rests on his texts alone. Thatcherism, ordoliberalism and authoritarian neoliberalism are separate entries. Hayek's and Friedman's money positions differ and Williamson's Washington Consensus is a description of institutional policy for Latin America, not a movement's programme.
